content: Before the advent of modern medicine, many mothers and their babies did not survive pregnancy or childbirth. However, with advancements in medical care, proper prenatal care can greatly enhance the health and outcomes for both the mother and the baby. Components of Good Prenatal Care: Maintaining proper nutrition and healthy habits both before and during pregnancy is essential. Regular prenatal check-ups are necessary to monitor the health of the mother and baby. Routine ultrasounds are performed to identify any potential issues with the baby. Screening tests are conducted to detect: Blood type incompatibilities, such as Rh or ABO issues. Gestational diabetes. Genetic disorders, especially if there is a family history or if the mother is of advanced maternal age. Immunity to rubella. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Protein levels in the urine, which may indicate preeclampsia or other conditions. Women planning to carry a pregnancy to term should select a healthcare provider who will oversee their prenatal care, delivery, and postpartum needs. Options for providers typically include: Obstetricians and gynecologists (OB/GYNs). Certified nurse midwives (CNMs). Family medicine physicians. Family nurse practitioners (FNPs) or physician assistants (PAs) working under a physician. Perinatologists, who specialize in managing high-risk pregnancies. For women with uncomplicated pregnancies, general family healthcare providers can manage care and delivery. If complications arise, a referral to a specialist will be made. Goals of Prenatal Care: Continuously monitor the health of both the mother and baby throughout the pregnancy. Identify any changes that could lead to a high-risk pregnancy. Provide guidance on nutritional needs during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Offer recommendations or restrictions regarding physical activity. Address and manage common pregnancy-related symptoms, such as morning sickness, back pain, leg discomfort, frequent urination, constipation, and heartburn, ideally without the use of medications. Offer emotional and informational support to the pregnant woman and her family. Women who are pregnant or planning to conceive should consume a balanced diet and take a vitamin and mineral supplement containing at least 0.4 milligrams (400 micrograms) of folic acid daily. Folic acid is crucial for reducing the risk of neural tube defects, such as spina bifida. In some cases, higher doses may be recommended for women at increased risk of these conditions. Pregnant women should avoid all medications unless deemed necessary and approved by their prenatal healthcare provider. It is important to discuss all medication use with a healthcare provider. Additionally, pregnant women should abstain from alcohol and drug use, limit caffeine intake, and refrain from smoking. Herbal supplements and over-the-counter medications that could interfere with fetal development should also be avoided. Prenatal Visit Schedule: During the first 28 weeks of pregnancy, visits are typically scheduled every 4 weeks. From 28 to 36 weeks of gestation, visits occur every 2-3 weeks. From 36 weeks until delivery, visits are scheduled weekly. At each visit, the following are usually assessed and recorded: Maternal weight gain. Fundal height (to assess uterine growth). The baby’s heartbeat (if appropriate). Routine urine tests may also be performed. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Schedule an appointment if you suspect you are pregnant, are currently pregnant but not receiving prenatal care, or are unable to manage common pregnancy symptoms without medication. Notify your provider if you are pregnant and have been exposed to sexually transmitted infections, harmful chemicals, radiation, or unusual pollutants. Seek medical attention if you are pregnant and develop a fever, chills, or painful urination. Emergency Situations: Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of the following during pregnancy: Vaginal bleeding of any amount. Severe abdominal pain. Physical trauma or severe emotional distress. Rupture of membranes (water breaking). If you are in the second half of your pregnancy and notice reduced or absent fetal movements, seek medical attention promptly.
